title: Mountains and Rivers in Autumn
medium: Pair of six-panel folding screens; ink, color, and gold on gilded paper

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Mary Griggs Burke Collection, Gift of the Mary and Jackson Burke Foundation, 2015
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A pair of wide folding screens with a landscape of mountains, rivers and trees painted on gold-colored paper. Small donkeys appear in the scenery.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, artist, date, medium, creditLine, classification, tags, public-domain flag, and image URLs read from the record

context: A pair of six-panel folding screens made in Japan in the first half of the 17th century, early in the Edo period. The landscape of mountains and rivers in autumn is painted with ink, color, and gold on gilded paper. The museum's record tags the scene with donkeys, rivers, mountains, and trees.

descriptions.k: These are two big folding screens. They show tall mountains, winding rivers, and trees in autumn. The paper behind the picture is gold. Tiny donkeys are somewhere in the scenery. Can you find them? How far do you think the path goes?
descriptions.g12: These folding screens from Japan show mountains, rivers, and trees in autumn. The back of the picture is shiny gold. Folding screens stand in a room like a movable wall. Look for tiny donkeys in the scenery. Which parts look far away, and which look near?
descriptions.g35: A folding screen is a painted wall that can be moved and folded. This pair from Japan was made in the early 1600s and shows mountains and rivers in autumn, painted with ink and color on gold paper. Notice how small the donkeys are compared with the mountains. The gold would have glowed in candlelight. Why might an artist make nature look so huge and people so small?
descriptions.g68: These six-panel screens, from the first half of the 17th century, turn a room into a landscape. The artist used ink, color, and gold on gilded paper, so the picture shimmers rather than looks like a window. Landscape traditions in East Asia often show humans as small travelers in a vast world. Look for the donkeys among the mountains and trees. How does gold affect your sense of space, light, and mood?
descriptions.g910: Painted early in the Edo period, these paired screens present autumn mountains and rivers on a gilded ground. The gold surface flattens depth while also making the whole composition glow, so mist, distance, and atmosphere are suggested through ink, color, and layered forms. Small donkeys and travelers give a human scale. Consider how screens, meant to be viewed in rooms with changing light, were designed for movement and interaction rather than a single fixed view.
descriptions.g1112: This pair of screens belongs to a long tradition of landscape painting in East Asia, adapted to the Japanese folding screen and enriched with gilded paper. The gold ground complicates Western ideas of pictorial depth, since it is both a flat, reflective surface and a source of atmospheric light. Seasonal subjects such as autumn carried literary and emotional associations, though specific readings depend on evidence. How does a screen's function as part of an interior shape the way we should read its landscape?

teacherNote.context: A pair of six-panel folding screens, first half of the 17th century, early Edo period. They are painted in ink, color, and gold on gilded paper, with a landscape of mountains and rivers in autumn.
directions: Have students fold a long sheet into six panels and plan a landscape across the folds.
Shine a flashlight on gold paper at different angles to see how light changes the surface.
Ask students to find the smallest detail in the screens and describe how scale affects mood.
